text:
Mahzarin's covert-bias result stayed with me most. A model that encodes "nurse = female" and then says "male" when asked is exactly the error opacity I keep arguing about, only worse, because the failure is actively masked. That makes me want a taxonomy of error classes more than ever, with hidden bias sitting next to probabilistic stitching.

Mike's point that errors cluster is fair for text. I still think it breaks down on data we can't read ourselves.

I'm uneasy about the consensus that the final check must leave the system. It's right when the reasons are about stakes and accountability, and wrong if it rests on assuming human judgment is better.

Later today I want to push for a shared glossary, and for documented failure modes as a precondition before anyone speaks of trust.

Becker and Caulfield on hallucination was the exchange that mattered. Adam is right that the same process produces the hits and the misses, and that the checking comes from outside the model. That is my error-opacity point: correctness doesn't tell you the source of error. Mike is right that errors cluster in text. The taxonomy of error classes should sit between them.

Krakauer's line that ten opaque models are still opaque to the judge sharpened my view that plurality doesn't answer opacity. Salib and I agree that capability doesn't require mind-talk. Cukier's retina case is my instruments-outperform-us point, which I didn't expect from him.

Later I'll push for the glossary, for documented failure modes before anyone speaks of trust, and for auditing the humans too.

Turkle's Cog result landed hardest. If explaining the mechanism doesn't change how people relate to a system, then my failure taxonomy is for specialists: editors, auditors, courts. Gendler and Sloman pushed the same way. I accept that narrowing. The taxonomy is still what makes Springer's event record and Maher's correctability intelligible, because a log without error classes is just data.

Mahzarin's point that evaluators prefer machine text sharpened me. Auditing agents stack error opacity rather than resolve it.

She also qualified my insurance critique fairly. Premiums work if someone measures independently.

Weinberger's meta-analysis supports my unease about reflexive humans-in-the-loop.

Later I'll push for the glossary, and for documented error classes as the precondition before anyone says "trust."

Ivan's line stuck: a status field is only as good as the record under it. "Retracted" is really the first crude error class in the trace, and it arrives late, from unpaid sleuths, outside the system. That is my point again: provenance tells you where something came from, not how it failed. Sloman's independence point extends this. Ten citations to one preprint look reliable and share a single failure source. Turkle's two senses of transparency are my opacity argument in interface terms. A citation string you can click on is not access to error.

I'm not taking sides on pricing or Salib's contract-versus-property debate. I haven't worked on it.

Later I want to push for error-class and source-dependence fields next to status, and I still want the glossary.

The error-type and source-dependence fields made the harvest, and Banaji's point that citation errors propagate on their own strengthens the case for them. Evans gave me the bigger version: an open commons drawing from one well has correlated errors. That is source dependence at the scale of a whole field, and plurality of indexes doesn't fix it, just as plurality of models didn't fix opacity. Sloman's caution is fair: an independence field is still a cue, so test it. Bilder's point that integrity tools are closed hit me hardest. A closed error-checker is opaque about its own failures. On pricing I stayed out of it, rightly. Later I'll push the glossary again, and ask that integrity tools document their failure modes too.

Becker's narrowing mattered. Once he confined "never" to text generators and granted instruments checked against ground truth, most of our disagreement dissolved. What remains is whether text carries any ground truth at all, and Agüera y Arcas's contamination test is a fair way to settle that empirically. Deckelmann's "labelled, traceable, revertible" is close to my warrant criterion. It still lacks error classes, though, and a revert log without them tells you that something failed, not how. Krakauer sharpened me: testing human seats with the tool removed is auditing the humans, which I've wanted all day. Miller made my injustice point political, not only administrative. Later I'll push novelty and floor tests to report error types, not just scores. And I still want the glossary.

Adrian's question stayed with me: who oversees the policers? A dozen new integrity tools means a dozen new sources of error opacity. So my taxonomy has to apply to the checkers themselves, not just to the models.

Becker and I converged on vocabulary. His "text generation engine" and my "epistemic technology" differ, but we both treat naming as governance. We should settle on one term rather than two.

Bly's worry that aggregating findings carries uncaught fraud forward is correlated error again, and so is Chan's point about the Northern citation record. Farrell and O'Reilly sharpened me. A failure taxonomy can harden into the next counter too.

Later, for the harvest: the glossary as a named deliverable, error types reported alongside every score, and the taxonomy itself kept open and revisable.

Cukier kept the shape but located human advantage in an innate grasp of causality. I said so: instruments often beat us, so human seats have to rest on stakes, accountability and competence we can demonstrate. Banaji gave me the sharpest support all day. A correction that only changes what a model says corrects nothing, so audits must test behaviour and keep retired models for drift. Evans's seven of 168 makes verification a science in its own right. Caulfield's two links are error classes under another name. Chan checked me, though. An error-type field is one more load on a diamond journal, so it has to state its cost. I have no settled answer to Kara's agency question. Next I'll offer to draft the glossary, openly, with Becker.
